en: Therein, first, at the time of beginning the construction of the maṇḍala house, having stabilized and cast two Brahma-lines upon a purified ground according to this procedure, and having subsequently made a mark at the southeast corner, the two Brahma-lines should be cast following that mark. The sequence for this is as follows:

First, at the time of commencing the construction of the mandala house, one should firmly establish and strike the two Brahma-lines upon a completely pure site according to this ritual procedure. Subsequently, one should mark the signs upon the moon-seats, and following those signs, the two Brahma-lines of the mandala should be struck. Regarding that, the sequence is as follows:
"Having first erected the kila, [one draws] a circle of one *vitasti*."
Having performed [the calculation] according to the sequence of the sun for both the emergence and entry of the shadow.
First, one should fashion a kīla of equal proportions, a single circle one span in height; then, by means of the sequence of the sun, [one observes] the coming and going of the shadow.
Having placed two dots on those two [ends], one should likewise place another of that same measure;
then, having fixed the thread at the dot, one should mark the "crow's foot" (*kākapāda*) along that thread.
How should one mark the ground?

In that place, one should apply two *bindus*; likewise, in other places as well, having fixed the *bindus*, one should draw the lines, and there one should make the marks following the path of a crow.
First, from the west and the east,
one should then project two Brahma-lines toward the south and the north, just like the two sky-lines.
First, to the west and the east; then again, to the south and the north. There, like a drop in the sky, one should draw two Brahma-lines.
Holding it with both hands extended equally, one should cause it to fall;
having again grasped the Brahma-thread, one should mark that as the "crow's foot" (kākapāda).
One should thoroughly strike those [lines] with hands held level; then, grasping the Brahma-line with the hand, one should mark it there following the path of the crow.
There, one should sequentially draw the two diagonal lines and the central line;
meanwhile, [the deity] sits in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), having placed the right foot down while the left remains drawn up.
These are the two lines for the center; one should also strike the root lines in succession. [The practitioner] sits with the left leg in the half-lotus posture and the right foot drawn in.

The wise Vajra-holder, together with a disciple who is seated in the opposite manner from that [of the teacher], should lay out the mandala by means of the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the space-thread (*khasūtra*). What wise person, together with a disciple, [should do so]? [The Vajra-holder. He should delineate the mandala through the conviction in the thread of space.
Having turned away from that, the wise disciple together [with the master] should perform the marking of the mandala lines with the vajra; they should apply themselves to the sword of the sky-line.
The same applies to other instances where a sutra is cited.
The same applies to the other [mandalas] as well for laying out the lines.
If the lines are not marked, there will be failure; if the cord is broken, the preceptor suffers loss.
From deficiency or excess, diseases arise; from confusion regarding the directions, the disciple becomes deluded.

Without the signs, accomplishment will not occur; if the marking thread is broken, the guru is exhausted; from deficiency or excess, illness arises; if the directions are confused, the disciple is deluded.

Having understood this and having exerted effort, if there should be no one suitable for laying the thread, then one should lay the thread oneself, having tied it to a stake, without depending on an assistant. (cf. VĀ verse: *If there should be no one suitable for laying the thread, then one should lay the thread oneself, having tied it to a stake, likewise without an assistant.*)

Having understood this, one should apply oneself with diligence. If, while laying out the lines, one lacks the necessary materials in some respect, or if one is without a companion or becomes displeased, then at that time, having bound the ritual peg (kīla), one should lay out the lines by oneself.
Standing there,
the wise preceptor, being well-composed, should together with the disciple cast the chalk-line according to this sequence.
Then, while the master and disciple remain together in profound meditative equipoise, the wise one should, according to this sequence, strike the white lines.
The preceptor, stationed in the west, and the disciple,
facing him while stationed here in the east, should cast down the Brahma-thread.
The preceptor who dwells by the water and the disciple who faces him—by remaining in the direction of Indra (the east), one should here strike the Brahma-line.
Standing in the direction of Yama (the south) together with a disciple who stands in the direction of Kubera (the north), the knower of mantras should correctly cast down the second Brahma-thread.
The disciple, together with one who possesses the secret mantra and vidyā residing in the direction of Yama and in the body of Virūpākṣa, shall correctly strike the second brahma-line.
When the preceptor is stationed in the southeast and the son is stationed in the northwest,
he who possesses the yoga of his own tutelary deity should cast the diagonal thread.

The preceptor residing at the intermediate points, together with those residing in the cardinal directions who are joined in the practice of their own tutelary deities, should strike the diagonal lines.
Standing in the northeastern direction, the preceptor,
together with the disciple, should correctly cast the second diagonal thread toward the southwestern direction.
From the direction of Īśāna, the Guru and the disciple who has gone to the direction of Vidyut should correctly strike the second diagonal line.
While the preceptor stands in the southeast and the disciple faces him,
standing in the northeast, he should cast the primary thread.

The disciple residing at the intermediate point and the disciple facing directly toward it—by means of these two disciples stationed at the intermediate points, the two fundamental lines should be drawn.
Remaining in that very place, the Vajrin, wise through gnosis, should cause the southern thread to fall by means of the son situated in the southwest.
In that very place, the wise one who knows the lines, being the son of the one dwelling in the Nairṛta [direction], should strike the southern line.
Remaining in that very position, the disciple, while the mantra-reciter stands at the northwest,
should cast the third thread, positioned between the southwest and the northwest.
The disciple should remain in that very place, and the mantrin should remain in the northwest; the third line should be drawn in the southwest, which is the direction of wind.
Remaining in that very [position], the Vajrin, who knows the ritual, should cause the fourth root-thread to fall by means of the son situated in the direction of Śiva.
At that very place, the one who possesses the vajra, having approached from the direction of peace with knowledge of the activities, should strike the fourth channel-line.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"First with the Brahma-line, second with the corner-lines."
With the third [line], one should cause four threads to fall on the four sides.
As the Blessed One taught in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "First is the Brahma-line; second is the diagonal line. On the third [stage], one should draw four lines upon the four sides."
Therefore, in this context, one-eighth of the root line is a *dvāra* (door); and a quarter of a *dvāra* is a *mātrā*, an *aṅgula*, a *kṛśa*, or a *bhāga*—these are synonyms.
In that regard, here, one-eighth of the root line is a *dvāra*; a portion of the *dvāra* is a *mātrā*, and *mātrā*, *prathama-bhāga*, *kṛśa*, and *bhāga* are its synonyms.
The *bhāga* consists of two morae (*dvimātrā*), the *mahābhāga* consists of four morae (*caturmātrā*), and *Śiva* is to be understood as half a mora (*ardhamātrā*).
The nature of two *cha chung* is a *cha*; four *cha chung* are one *cha chen*. Regarding "peaceful," it should be viewed as half a *cha chung*. This is the ritual for applying the white drops.
Thus concludes the procedure for laying out the lines with chalk. || 0 ||
